topics.title: Definition and Scope of the French Revolution
topics.summary: The French Revolution (1789‑1799) was a radical upheaval that ended absolute monarchy, abolished feudal privileges, and established citizenship and inalienable rights, spanning from the Estates‑General meeting to Napoleon’s coup of 18 Brumaire.

topics.title: The Ancien Régime and Social Structure
topics.summary: Pre‑revolutionary France was organized into three Estates—clergy, nobility, and the Third Estate (≈98 % of the population)—with the first two enjoying tax exemptions while the Third bore the fiscal burden.

topics.title: Long‑Term and Immediate Causes
topics.summary: Financial crisis from war debts, Enlightenment ideas, economic hardship after poor harvests, and weak royal leadership combined to trigger revolutionary pressure.

topics.title: The Estates‑General and the Birth of the National Assembly
topics.summary: Louis XVI convened the Estates‑General in May 1789; a dispute over voting led the Third Estate to proclaim itself the National Assembly on 17 June 1789.

topics.title: The Tennis Court Oath
topics.summary: Locked out of their meeting hall, deputies swore on 20 June 1789 at a tennis court to remain united until France had a constitution.

topics.title: The Storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear
topics.summary: On 14 July 1789 Parisians stormed the Bastille, a symbol of royal tyranny, while rural peasants reacted to rumors of aristocratic plots in the Great Fear.

topics.title: The Constitutional Monarchy (1789‑1792)
topics.summary: The National Assembly introduced reforms—departmental reorganization, the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and the 1791 Constitution—creating a limited monarchy that collapsed after the 1792 war defeats and the Tuileries storming.

topics.title: The Republic and the Reign of Terror (1792‑1794)
topics.summary: After abolishing the monarchy, the National Convention executed Louis XVI, created the Committee of Public Safety, and instituted the Reign of Terror, which claimed roughly 16‑17 000 lives.
topics.section_ref: Chapter 4: The Republic and the Terror, 1792-1794

topics.title: The Thermidorian Reaction and the Directory (1794‑1799)
topics.summary: Robespierre’s fall on 27 July 1794 ushered in a moderate Thermidorian regime, followed by the Directory—a corrupt, financially unstable government that lasted until Napoleon’s 1799 coup.
topics.section_ref: Chapter 5: Thermidor, the Directory, and Legacy

topics.title: Legacy of the French Revolution
topics.summary: The Revolution spread ideas of legal equality, national citizenship, secular governance, and constitutionalism, while also demonstrating how revolutions can devolve into violence and authoritarianism.
topics.section_ref: Chapter 5: Thermidor, the Directory, and Legacy

flashcards.question: Name two cultural or social reforms introduced by the Republic.
flashcards.answer: The Republican Calendar (1793) and the metric system; also a campaign of de‑Christianization and the 1794 abolition of slavery in French colonies.
flashcards.section_tag: Cultural and Social Changes

flashcards.question: What are the start and end dates commonly used to define the French Revolution?
flashcards.answer: It is usually dated from the meeting of the Estates‑General on 5 May 1789 to Napoleon’s coup of 18 Brumaire (9 November 1799).
flashcards.section_tag: Definition and Scope of the French Revolution

flashcards.question: On what date was Louis XVI executed, and what impact did his execution have internationally?
flashcards.answer: He was executed on 21 January 1793; the execution alarmed European monarchies and intensified the wars against France.
flashcards.section_tag: Execution of the King

flashcards.question: What was the outcome of the Flight to Varennes in June 1791 for the monarchy?
flashcards.answer: The royal family’s failed escape damaged trust in Louis XVI and weakened the monarchy’s legitimacy.
flashcards.section_tag: Flight to Varennes and the Constitution of 1791

flashcards.question: What political system was created by the Constitution of 1791?
flashcards.answer: A constitutional monarchy with a Legislative Assembly and a king who retained a suspensive veto; voting was limited to ‘active citizens’ who paid a minimum tax.
flashcards.section_tag: Flight to Varennes and the Constitution of 1791

flashcards.question: List three lasting legacies of the French Revolution.
flashcards.answer: Ideas of legal equality before the law, national citizenship, secular government, and the spread of written constitutions worldwide.
flashcards.section_tag: Legacy of the French Revolution

flashcards.question: Name two financial causes that contributed to the French Revolution.
flashcards.answer: Heavy state debt from supporting the American Revolution and chronic fiscal deficits that required half of the royal budget for debt service.
flashcards.section_tag: Long‑Term and Immediate Causes

flashcards.question: Which Enlightenment thinkers promoted ideas that influenced the Revolution?
flashcards.answer: Voltaire, Montesquieu, and Rousseau.
flashcards.section_tag: Long‑Term and Immediate Causes

flashcards.question: What were the three Estates of the Ancien Régime and which estate comprised about 98 % of the population?
flashcards.answer: First Estate – clergy; Second Estate – nobility; Third Estate – everyone else (peasants, merchants, etc.), which made up roughly 98 % of the population.
flashcards.section_tag: The Ancien Régime and Social Structure

flashcards.question: What was the Committee of Public Safety and who dominated it?
flashcards.answer: Created in April 1793 to protect the Republic; it was dominated by Maximilien Robespierre and the Jacobins.
flashcards.section_tag: The Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror

flashcards.question: Approximately how many people were officially sentenced to death during the Reign of Terror?
flashcards.answer: Historians estimate about 16,000‑17,000 official death sentences, with many more dying in prisons or in the Vendée.
flashcards.section_tag: The Committee of Public Safety and the Reign of Terror

flashcards.question: When did Napoleon Bonaparte seize power and what government did he establish?
flashcards.answer: On 9 November 1799 (18 Brumaire), he led a coup that overthrew the Directory and created the Consulate.
flashcards.section_tag: The Rise of Napoleon

flashcards.question: What event on 14 July 1789 is celebrated as France’s national day?
flashcards.answer: The storming of the Bastille.
flashcards.section_tag: The Storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear

flashcards.question: When was the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen adopted and what core rights did it proclaim?
flashcards.answer: Adopted on 26 August 1789; it proclaimed liberty, property, security, resistance to oppression, and that sovereignty resides in the nation.
flashcards.section_tag: The Storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear

flashcards.question: What was the significance of the August 4, 1789 decrees for the feudal system?
flashcards.answer: They abolished feudal privileges and the tithe, effectively ending the legal framework of feudalism in France.
flashcards.section_tag: The Storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear

flashcards.question: What did the August 4, 1789 decrees accomplish?
flashcards.answer: They abolished feudal privileges and the tithe, ending the legal basis of the feudal system.
flashcards.section_tag: The Storming of the Bastille and the Great Fear

flashcards.question: What was the significance of the Tennis Court Oath on 20 June 1789?
flashcards.answer: Deputies pledged not to disband until France had a written constitution, marking a unified revolutionary commitment.
flashcards.section_tag: The Tennis Court Oath

flashcards.question: What event on 27 July 1794 (9 Thermidor Year II) marked the end of the Terror?
flashcards.answer: The Thermidorian Reaction: Robespierre was arrested and guillotined the next day, ending the Terror.
flashcards.section_tag: The Thermidorian Reaction

flashcards.question: What were the main weaknesses of the Directory (1795‑1799)?
flashcards.answer: Corruption, financial instability, and heavy reliance on the army.
flashcards.section_tag: The Thermidorian Reaction and the Directory

flashcards.question: When was the monarchy formally abolished and the First French Republic proclaimed?
flashcards.answer: The monarchy was abolished and the Republic proclaimed on 21‑22 September 1792 by the National Convention.
flashcards.section_tag: War and the Fall of the Monarchy

flashcards.question: Which two major wars began during the Revolutionary period and in what years?
flashcards.answer: The French Revolutionary Wars began with France declaring war on Austria in April 1792; later, the War in the Vendée (a civil war) erupted in 1793.
flashcards.section_tag: War and the Fall of the Monarchy

flashcards.question: Which event on 10 August 1792 led to the suspension of the king?
flashcards.answer: Crowds, including sans‑culottes, stormed the Tuileries Palace, forcing the suspension of Louis XVI.
flashcards.section_tag: War and the Fall of the Monarchy
